questions.question: Define afterload? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Define Afterload
  • • Afterload is the pressure or resistance the ventricles must overcome to
  • eject blood during systole.
  • • It is mainly determined by arterial blood pressure and vascular resistance.
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026

questions.question: Explain how an increase in vascular resistance affects blood pressure. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• How does an increase in vascular resistance affect blood pressure?
  • • Increased vascular resistance makes it harder for blood to flow through
  • vessels.
  • • This increases arterial blood pressure because the heart must pump against
  • greater resistance.

questions.question: Explain the importance of ventricular diastole in the cardiac cycle. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the importance of ventricular diastole in the cardiac cycle.
  • • Ventricular diastole is the relaxation phase of the ventricles.
  • • It allows ventricular filling with blood from the atria.
  • • Adequate filling ensures an optimal stroke volume during the next
  • contraction.

questions.question: How does increased afterload influence stroke volume? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• How does increased afterload influence stroke volume?
  • • Increased afterload makes it more difficult for the heart to eject blood.
  • • As a result, stroke volume decreases if cardiac contractility does not
  • increase.

  • oxygen availability.
  • • Aerobic zone training involves moderate-intensity exercise where oxygen
  • supply meets demand.
  • • Anaerobic training improves power and speed, while aerobic training
  • improves endurance.

questions.question: Define energy expenditure and explain its relationship with heart rate during exercise. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Define energy expenditure and explain its relationship with heart rate during
  • exercise.
  • • Energy Expenditure: The amount of energy used by the body to perform
  • physical activity and maintain bodily functions.
  • • Relationship with Heart Rate:
  • • Heart rate increases as exercise intensity increases.
  • • Higher intensity requires greater energy expenditure.
  • • Increased oxygen demand causes the heart to pump faster.
  • • Therefore, heart rate is often used to estimate energy expenditure.
  • • There is a near-linear relationship between heart rate and oxygen
  • consumption during moderate exercise.

questions.question: Explain how electrical impulses are generated and conducted through the heart to produce coordinated cardiac contraction. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain how electrical impulses are generated and conducted through the
  • heart.
  • • Electrical impulses originate in the Sinoatrial (SA) Node, the heart's
  • natural pacemaker.
  • • The impulse spreads through both atria causing atrial contraction.
  • • It reaches the Atrioventricular (A V) Node, where a brief delay occurs.
  • • The impulse then travels through the Bundle of His.
  • • It continues through the right and left bundle branches.
  • • Finally, Purkinje fibers distribute the impulse throughout the ventricles.
  • • This coordinated conduction produces synchronized ventricular
  • contraction.

questions.question: Describe the factors affecting ventricular filling time. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the factors affecting ventricular filling time.
  • • Heart Rate: Increased heart rate reduces filling time.
  • • Venous Return: Greater venous return increases ventricular filling.
  • • Atrial Contraction: Enhances ventricular filling.
  • • Ventricular Compliance: More compliant ventricles fill more easily.
  • • Blood V olume: Increased blood volume improves filling.
  • • Duration of Diastole: Longer diastole allows greater filling.

questions.question: Define cardiac output. Explain the formula used to calculate cardiac output and describe its normal resting values. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Define cardiac output. Explain the formula and normal resting values.
  • • Cardiac output is the volume of blood pumped by the heart per minute.
  • • Formula CO = HR × SV
  • • CO = Cardiac Output
  • • HR = Heart Rate
  • • SV = Stroke V olume
  • • Normal Resting Values
  • • Average resting heart rate = 70–75 bpm.
  • • Average stroke volume = 70 mL/beat.
  • • Normal resting cardiac output ≈ 5 L/min.
  • • May increase to 20–40 L/min during intense exercise.
